item.title: 6.7 magnitude earthquake hits Peru
item.description: A 6.7-magnitude earthquake struck central Peru on Friday, Peru’s Defense Ministry said, with preliminary reports indicating minor damage and no fatalities. The earthquake occurred at 7:09 pm (0009 GMT Saturday), 30 kilometers (18 miles) northwest of the city of Junin, at a depth of 129 kilometers. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) also measured the quake to have a magnitude of 6.7, but estimated its depth to be only 108 kilometers. Peru’s Defense Minister, Rafael Belaunde, reported that after the earthquake “minor damage was reported to homes in different parts of Junin, as well as interruptions of electricity service and restrictions on highway transit.” Belaunde added that there had been “no harm to people or impacts to their bodies and health.” AFP journalists in Lima saw hundreds of people evacuating buildings in the Miraflores district during the quake. The earthquake was also felt in the capital Lima, as well as Ancash, Ica, Ucayali, Cerro de Pasco, Huanuco and Callao. Peru’s National Emergency Operation Center (COEN) reported the quake was felt with moderate to strong intensity and that “monitoring continues in vulnerable areas.” Hernando Tavera, the president of the Peruvian Geophysical Institute, told AFP: “The ground shaking was intense. We have no reports of damage at the moment, but there have been landslides and rockfalls on the hillsides.” Peru is situated on the so-called Pacific Ring of Fire — an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin. Seismologists say Peru experiences at least 400 earthquakes per year, three-quarters of which are so weak people do not feel them. A 5.1-magnitude earthquake in the Junin region in July killed six people, injured 32 others and destroyed 52 homes. item.title: Why obesity hits men harder than women – Study
item.description: By Shola Ogundipe Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological difference in the fat tissue of males and females that could help explain why obesity triggers different health consequences in men and women. The discovery suggests that the battle against obesity may be playing out differently beneath the skin, with immune cells living inside body fat either helping to protect against inflammation and metabolic disorders or making them worse, depending on biological sex. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside, US, found that a group of immune cells known as eosinophils, traditionally associated with allergies and asthma, perform different functions in the fat tissue of male and female mice. While certain populations of these cells appear to protect against obesity-related inflammation, others may contribute to harmful metabolic changes. The study, titled “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity”, was funded by the National Institutes of Health, the UCR School of Medicine and the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine. The findings, published in the journal PNAS Nexus, challenge the longstanding assumption that eosinophils are largely similar in structure and function. They also raise questions about whether obesity treatments targeting the immune system should be designed differently for men and women. Led by biomedical scientists Meera Nair and Adam Godzik, the study used high-resolution single-cell sequencing to examine how individual immune cells behave in fat tissue. What emerged was an unexpected picture. The researchers identified six distinct populations of eosinophils in adipose tissue, each with its own genetic activity and potentially different biological functions. The discovery suggests that these cells are not simply passive occupants of body fat. Some may help maintain metabolic health, while others may contribute to the inflammatory processes associated with obesity. “Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at UCR’s School of Medicine. She explained that identifying and activating the biological pathways responsible for producing protective eosinophils could open new possibilities for improving metabolic health. But perhaps the most striking finding was the difference between male and female mice. Female mice had a population of eosinophils that appeared to work more effectively with macrophages, another group of immune cells found in fat tissue. Their cooperation seemed to support a healthier environment within fat tissue and better metabolic function. Male mice, however, showed a different response when exposed to a high-fat diet. They were more likely to develop eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, alongside weaker protective activity in their fat tissue. item.title: Delta: Six suspects in custody, no justice yet for Adeda?
item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi From a workplace assault to justice in limbo, family grief and fears deepen 58 days after death of a Delta State Deputy Director. Fifty-eight days after Unity Ekwevugbe Adeda died following a brutal workplace assault in Asaba, Delta State, six suspects remain in police custody, but no charges have been filed and no autopsy conducted to establish precise medical cause of death. For the Adeda family of Otovwodo, Ughelli, the prolonged wait for answers is deepening their grief and fears that those responsible for the death of their son could escape justice. Adeda, a Level 16 Deputy Director in the Department of Examination and Standards, Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education, died on September 24, 2026, following a physical altercation at his workplace. His death triggered protests by civil servants. It led to the constitution of an administrative panel of inquiry by the Delta State Government. The police also commenced separate criminal investigation. But nearly two months after the incident, the family and concerned stakeholders are asking what progress has been made towards prosecution. Six Suspects, No Charges The police investigation, handled by the Homicide Section of the State Criminal Investigation Department, has resulted in six arrests, including Dr. Kingsley Ashibogwu, Commissioner for Secondary Education, and Mrs Clementine Ufuoma, Director of Basic and Secondary Education. The arrests began with Lucky Adoh, an aide to the commissioner, shortly after the incident. Ashibogwu and three other suspects were subsequently taken into custody, bringing the number to five. Ufuoma, earlier declared wanted, later surrendered, increasing the number to six. Despite the arrests, no formal charges have been announced. Under the criminal justice process, the police are expected to conclude investigations, compile their findings and forward the duplicate case file to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), Ministry of Justice, for legal advice. The DPP is expected to examine the evidence and determine whether a prima facie case exists to warrant formal charges. However, the process has yet to reach that stage publicly, leaving questions about when the investigation will be concluded. For Austine Aghomi, Coordinator, Journalists for Just Development of the Niger Delta, the silence of the police and the delay in providing meaningful updates are increasingly troubling. He said: “But more concerning is the arrested progress on the part of the police. When will investigations be concluded? “Can’t prosecution progress with a few other suspects still at large? Where is the autopsy to determine or confirm Adeda’s true cause of death after the assault? “The police have not helped this case at all and it is just another test of integrity, seeing the police mum on this case for so long without offering meaningful updates. “It’s like a conspiracy theory is building over this matter. item.title: No roof for two masters, by Stephanie Shaakaa
item.description: * Bloodline, Ballot Box, and the Bedroom: Lessons from Kano’s High Stakes Political Divorce A marriage rarely belongs to two people alone. In northern Nigeria, where zumunci binds families through kinship, mutual obligations and family honour, marriage often carries expectations that extend far beyond the couple. For twenty years, the union between Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf and Zainab Musa Kwankwaso appeared to demonstrate that bloodline and political loyalty could coexist under one roof. Today, that roof has given way. The breakdown of the marriage between Governor Yusuf and Zainab, niece of his estranged political mentor, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, and raised in the former governor’s household, is more than a headline from Government House. It raises an uncomfortable question: what happens when the political alliance connecting two families collapses, but the marriage binding them is left caught in its aftermath? To understand the significance of this separation, one must understand how political trust is built in Kano. Political relationships are not always sustained by ambition and party loyalty alone. Sometimes, they are reinforced through family connections. When Zainab and Abba Yusuf married on July 29, 2006, Yusuf was already deeply embedded in Kwankwaso’s political circle, having served as his personal and special assistant during Kwankwaso’s first tenure as governor and subsequently during his tenure as Minister of Defence. Zainab, raised in Kwankwaso’s household, was not simply marrying an ambitious politician. Their union connected two families whose fortunes were closely intertwined. Over twenty years and six children, the marriage became one of the most personal bonds surrounding the Kwankwasiyya movement. Yusuf’s years of loyalty and proximity to Kwankwaso eventually culminated in his emergence as the latter’s preferred successor and his election as governor in 2023. The trusted lieutenant had become governor, with the backing of the political establishment that had shaped his career. Yet there is a particular difficulty with marriages surrounded by powerful family and political networks. The expectations attached to them can become difficult to separate from the personal commitments of the couple. While everyone shares the same interests, the arrangement may appear harmonious. The real test comes when those interests begin to diverge. That divergence became unmistakable in January 2026, when Governor Yusuf abandoned the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP), the platform on which he won office, and defected to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). The decision marked a decisive break with Kwankwaso, the political mentor who had nurtured his rise. With Kwankwaso pursuing a different political direction ahead of the 2027 elections, an alliance that once united two households became a bitter contest over Kano’s political future. item.title: Do women control their husbands?
item.description: By Chioma Gabriel, Editor, Special Features It is often said that women are a necessary evil, a desirable calamity and a domestic peril. It all depends on where one is standing. In traditional African societies, a woman’s place was said to be in the kitchen, from where she was expected to work her way into her husband’s heart through his stomach. Women were traditionally expected to be seen but not heard. They were like shadows trailing their husbands, with little or no opportunity to express opinions on matters affecting the family and society. They were often regarded as acquired possessions whose primary responsibilities were to bear children and provide labour on the farms. They had little or no say in the scheme of things. A similar pattern appears in some biblical accounts, where headcounts excluded women and children. When Jesus fed the 5,000 and the 4,000, the recorded figures referred to the men, with women and children excluded from the count. In the early Christian community, Paul’s instruction required women to remain silent in church and ask their husbands questions at home. Although interpretations of this passage differ among Christian scholars, it has historically been cited to support restrictions on women’s public religious participation. Despite these historical and cultural limitations, women have, in different ways, exercised considerable influence over men, including their husbands. Biblical accounts The Bible contains several accounts of women whose actions, decisions or influence significantly shaped the lives of men. Eve persuaded Adam to eat the forbidden fruit after the serpent tempted her in the Garden of Eden. Jezebel manipulated her husband, King Ahab, and orchestrated the murder of Naboth to acquire his vineyard. Delilah used persistent pressure and deception to make Samson reveal the secret of his extraordinary strength. Sapphira conspired with her husband, Ananias, to deceive the apostles about the proceeds from the sale of their property. Michal helped David escape from King Saul but later confronted and despised him over his public dancing before God. Bathsheba, working alongside the prophet Nathan, intervened to ensure that David fulfilled his promise that Solomon would succeed him as king. Sarah persuaded Abraham to have a child through her maidservant, Hagar, and later demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. Rebekah orchestrated a family deception by persuading her son Jacob to disguise himself as Esau and obtain Isaac’s blessing. Herodias influenced her daughter to demand the head of John the Baptist from her husband, Herod Antipas. Job’s wife, overwhelmed by their suffering, urged her husband to curse God and die. Mary and Martha also demonstrated the emotional influence women could have. When their brother, Lazarus, died, their grief deeply moved Jesus, who wept before raising him from the dead. item.title: Infantino hails Warri Stadium, wants football in every community
item.description: FIFA President Gianni Infantino has praised the renovated Warri City Stadium in Delta State, saying football development must extend beyond major stadiums to local communities. Infantino spoke during a visit to Warri, where he attended the commissioning of the renovated stadium and upgraded sporting facilities. The FIFA president said football should be accessible to everyone, regardless of their location, adding that smaller stadiums play an important role in bringing the sport closer to communities. “Yeah, that’s what football is about, isn’t it? It’s for everyone, everywhere,” Infantino told reporters in Warri yesterday. “It’s big stadiums, it’s the World Cup, but it’s also smaller stadiums. It’s the proximity, and to be here in Warri for me is a fantastic occasion to showcase what we are about in FIFA, what we are about in football.” Infantino also expressed appreciation for the warm reception he received in Nigeria and across Africa, attributing the relationship to years of collaboration and football development projects aimed at improving the lives of young people. “Oh yes, I’m feeling so much the love of Africa, the love of Nigeria. This is based, of course, on many years of joint life together, of projects that we’ve put in place, of changing lives of girls and boys,” he said. item.title: Hamzat seeks stronger collaboration to accelerate Lagos’ digital transformation
item.description: ​‌‌​⁠‌​‍⁠⁠‍‍⁠​‍‍‍​‍‌​ Lagos State Deputy Gov. Obafemi Hamzat has called for stronger collaboration among research institutions, government and the private sector to commercialise innovations, strengthen the economy and accelerate Lagos’ digital transformation. Hamzat made the call at a private fintech town hall convened by MyCard Global, a fintech company, in collaboration with the Fintech Association of Nigeria held in Lagos on Friday. The town hall had the theme, “The Lagos Digital Economy Blueprint: Co-Authoring the Lagos Digital Economy Agenda”. It brought together government officials, fintech leaders, technology companies, investors and other stakeholders to discuss how the private sector could contribute to shaping the state’s digital economy. The deputy governor at the meeting, outlined the state’s efforts to integrate research, technology, data infrastructure, innovation and enterprise development into governance and economic growth. Hamzat said that Lagos had continued to support science-based research through a platform that brought young innovators forward to present ideas for funding. He added that the state needed to strengthen the mechanism for translating research into commercial products and services. He said that the state needed to move beyond fragmented, government-funded projects toward a coordinated innovation ecosystem capable of connecting research, incubation, funding, industries and commercialisation. Hamzat, who was also a former Commissioner for Science and Technology, stressed the importance of reliable data in planning. He described data as critical to determining the actual needs of residents and ensuring that government projects were properly targeted. Hamzat said that the state was seeking to move from disconnected programmes and individual initiatives to an integrated data-driven governance system. According to him, the system will be capable of supporting planning, research, innovation and economic development. He said that the government was also working toward expanding its digital infrastructure. ‘’This includes fibre-optic connectivity, from the existing 2,400 kilometres to about 6,000 kilometres, through partnerships with telecommunications companies and other private-sector stakeholders. ‘’The infrastructure expansion is expected to connect schools, public institutions and other facilities, improve access to digital services and reduce the cost of doing business, ‘’ he said. Hamzat said that the state was connecting educational institutions and renovating infrastructure to ensure that students and public institutions had improved access to internet services. According to him, the ultimate objective is to connect all public schools. Hamzat further said that the state was also working toward strengthening data governance and standardisation. item.title: Lagos renews campaign against open defecation
item.description: …Calls for improved sanitation, gender-sensitive toilet facilities By Olasunkanmi Akoni The Lagos State Government has renewed its campaign for improved sanitation, proper hygiene practices and access to safe toilet facilities as part of efforts to eliminate open defecation and promote public health. The Special Adviser to the Governor on Environment, Olakunle Akodu, and the Permanent Secretary, Office of Environmental Services, Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources, Tajudeen Gaji, made the call on Friday as the state joined the rest of the world to commemorate World Toilet Day at Alausa, Ikeja. The 2026 celebration was held under the theme, “Sanitation and Gender Equality.” Akodu said women and girls required toilet facilities that guaranteed adequate privacy, reliable water supply, handwashing stations and hygienic conditions. He noted that Lagos’ growing population, rapid urbanisation and expanding commercial activities had placed enormous pressure on existing sanitation infrastructure. According to him, addressing the challenges requires deliberate public policies, sustained capital investment, institutional discipline and collective civic responsibility. He said the state government recognised that a clean, resilient and sustainable environment must guarantee every resident access to safe, dignified and functional sanitation facilities. Earlier, Gaji, who was represented by the Director of Sanitation Services, Hassan Sanuth, said the commemoration underscored the importance of proper sanitation in preventing diseases, protecting public health and promoting a cleaner environment. He described access to safe toilets as more than a basic necessity, saying it was fundamental to human dignity and public health. Gaji said sanitation was closely linked to personal security, social equality and the fundamental right of every citizen to live in a healthy environment. He warned that inadequate access to safe and private toilet facilities could undermine people’s health, security, dignity, education and participation in economic and social activities. The permanent secretary therefore called for inclusive policies and investments that would address the sanitation needs of women, girls, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups. item.title: Waste crisis: LAWMA acting MD unveils 60-day action plan
item.description: …Warns staff against laxity, promises operational overhaul By Olasunkanmi Akoni The newly appointed Acting Managing Director of the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), Olajuwon Akinyemi, has unveiled a 60-day emergency action plan to tackle waste management challenges across Lagos State, warning staff against indiscipline and poor performance. Akinyemi, who has assumed office amid growing concerns over waste accumulation across the metropolis, said the plan was aimed at clearing waste backlogs, strengthening regulatory enforcement and restoring the agency’s operational efficiency. He disclosed this on Friday while addressing management and staff at a workers’ forum held at LAWMA’s headquarters in Ijora-Olopa, Lagos. Accompanied by the Acting Executive Director, Operations, Dr. Olorunwa Tijani, and the Executive Director, Finance, Kunle Adebiyi, the acting managing director called for renewed commitment, discipline and professionalism among workers. He said repositioning the agency would require active participation and dedication from personnel at all levels. “We are bringing in resilience and a new paradigm shift. It is a new wave in handling waste in Lagos. “We already have the template to transform LAWMA positively. All we need to do is recreate, modernise and do better than in the past,” Akinyemi said. Outlining the 60-day action plan, he said personnel would be redeployed across the state’s three operational districts based on their familiarity with the respective areas to strengthen field monitoring and improve response times. He also announced plans to establish decentralised operational hubs to improve supervision, facilitate faster interventions and address waste disposal blackspots across the state. On indiscriminate waste disposal, Akinyemi said the agency would intensify public enlightenment on waste sorting at source and responsible disposal practices. He said traditional rulers, Community Development Association (CDA) leaders, market associations and artisans would be mobilised to promote compliance with proper waste management practices. The acting managing director also called for stronger collaboration with Private Sector Participation (PSP) operators and urged residents to comply with approved waste collection tariffs to sustain service delivery. On staff welfare, Akinyemi assured workers that their well-being remained a priority, disclosing that efforts were underway to procure Compressed Natural Gas (CNG)-powered buses to address transportation challenges. Earlier, Tijani called for urgent action to revitalise LAWMA’s operational framework, saying the agency needed an immediate overhaul to improve field performance. Similarly, Adebiyi said the success of the 60-day plan would depend on prudent financial management, accountability and effective collaboration across the agency’s directorates. item.title: CONTTA: Varsity health workers petition education minister over NSIWC exclusion
item.description: By Ebunoluwa Sessou The Coalition of Healthcare Professionals in Tertiary Education Institutions of Nigeria, CHPTEIN, has petitioned the Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, demanding the suspension of a circular issued by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission,NSIWC allegedly excluding healthcare workers in federal universities from the payment of the Consolidated Tertiary Institutions Teaching Allowance, CONTTA. The coalition, representing affected medical doctors, nurses, pharmacists, medical laboratory scientists and other allied health professionals under the Consolidated Health Salary Structure, CONHESS and Consolidated Medical Salary Structure, CONMESS, also faulted widespread media reports describing the CONTTA payments as “excess payments” and subject to recovery. In an emergency petition delivered to the minister on Thursday, November 19, 2026, CHPTEIN rejected the characterisation, insisting that the payments were based on verified payroll computations by the Budget Office of the Federation and covered all eligible non-teaching staff in federal universities, irrespective of union affiliation. The petition challenged NSIWC Circular Ref: SWC/S/04/S.149/T/187, dated November 11, 2026, which the coalition said unlawfully excluded CONHESS and CONMESS healthcare workers from the CONTTA payment arrangement. Copies of the petition were also served on the Minister of Labour and Employment, Dr Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi; the Director-General of the Budget Office of the Federation; and the Chairman of NSIWC. The coalition argued that the November 11 circular directly contradicted an earlier directive by the Federal Ministry of Education, dated October 16, 2026, with reference number FME/TE/SS.IM/C./Vol.I/6. According to CHPTEIN, the ministry’s directive explicitly confirmed that the Budget Office of the Federation calculated the financial implications of CONTTA based on the entire workforce of non-teaching staff on the payroll, covering the payment of allowances to all non-teaching staff irrespective of their union affiliation. The coalition quoted the ministry’s clarification as stating: “The Budget Office of the Federation calculated the financial implications of CONTTA based on the entire workforce of the Non-teaching staff on the payroll… covering the payment of allowances of all Non-teaching staff irrespective of their union affiliation.” It questioned how NSIWC could unilaterally override the position of the supervising ministry, particularly when the funds had already been budgeted and released for all non-teaching workers on the nominal roll. CHPTEIN also called on the education minister to immediately suspend Circular Ref: SWC/S/04/S.149/T/187 and direct vice-chancellors and bursars in the 15 federal universities that had complied with the payment directive to halt the enforcement of NSIWC’s proposed three-month recovery of payments already made to affected healthcare workers. item.title: Peter Obi Will Win 2027 Election, What Happened In 2023 Won’t Repeat Itself — Babachir Lawal
item.description: A former Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF) and chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Babachir Lawal, has reiterated that the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, will win the 2027 general election, insisting that the circumstances surrounding the 2023 presidential poll will not be repeated. Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday, Lawal predicted that Obi would emerge victorious, expressing the belief that the political dynamics of the next election would be different from those of 2023. ﻿ He also questioned the outcome of the 2023 presidential election, arguing that there should have been a runoff as Obi got the highest number of votes, a development he believes would have changed the political calculations surrounding the contest. “Peter got the majority of votes; he didn’t get the spread. Bola Tinubu got the spread and came second. There should have been a runoff in that election,” he maintained. The former SGF further projected that Obi would win Kogi, Benue and Plateau states, while defeating former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in his home state of Adamawa. “I give it to you that Peter didn’t have more spread. This time, Peter will get the spread in Nigeria. “Atiku will come third in Adamawa State this time around,” he added. On the ADC candidate’s chances in the forthcoming election, Lawal argued that the former vice president would not have sufficient ethnic support to secure the presidency. Comparing the NDC ticket with those of other political parties, he described it as a better option. Lawal also disclosed that the party’s campaign strategy would prioritise town hall meetings, which he considers a more effective means of engaging voters. He said Nigerians would look in the direction of Obi due to his character and competence. “First of all, he is incorruptible. Second, he is detribalised. Third, he is a businessman that understands market forces. And fourth, he is a man who sticks to his words,” the NDC chieftain added. Asked whether the former Anambra State governor made any promises to him, the former SGF said, “No, he doesn’t need to”. The 72-year-old said he would go back to his 4,000 hectares of farmland where he produces cash crops and livestock, and watch Nigeria grow. Asked whether he does not want to partake in Obi’s government if he wins, Babachir said, “I’m 72 years old. I have a 40-year-old son. What is wrong if Peter says, ‘I’m going to make you Minister of Agric,’ and I say Peter, instead, give my son Minister of Agric. Is that wrong? In those days when we were young, that’s how things were done.” The post Peter Obi Will Win 2027 Election, What Happened In 2023 Won’t Repeat Itself — Babachir Lawal appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: [VIDEO] I Would’ve Advised El-Rufai To Talk Less If I Had Had Contact With Him — Yahaya Bello
item.description: Former Kogi State Governor, Yahaya Bello, has said he would have advised former Kaduna State governor, Nasir El-Rufai, to speak less if he had had the opportunity to speak with him before his legal battle began. Bello, who spoke during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday, said he would have urged El-Rufai to talk less, remain in the All Progressives Congress (APC) that he helped build, and wait to see what President Bola Tinubu would do. He described El-Rufai as a respected and idealistic person who pursues whatever he believes in. Bello said that though he does not wish him “to go down the drain,” the embattled former Kaduna governor must have learnt how to handle political differences. El-Rufai is facing legal battles involving the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) and the Department of State Services (DSS), alongside allegations of financial misconduct and unlawful phone interception. In October, the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal against the refusal of bail in the alleged financial misconduct case, upholding his continued detention by the ICPC. In a separate DSS prosecution over alleged unlawful interception of National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu’s telephone communications, the Federal High Court on October 26 dismissed his no-case submission and ordered him to enter his defence, adjourning proceedings to November 25. The Kaduna corruption trial, involving an alleged ₦8.68 billion CCTV contract, was adjourned to December 8, while a ₦1 billion fundamental rights suit against the ICPC, police and AGF is scheduled for judgment on December 2. item.title: I’m The Most Transparent, Vilified But I Shall Be Vindicated — Yahaya Bello
item.description: Former Kogi State Governor, Yahaya Bello, has expressed confidence that he will eventually be vindicated over the allegations of financial misconduct levelled against him by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). He also described himself as the most transparent individual. “I am the most transparent and the most vilified. But at the end of the day, I shall be vindicated,” Bello said on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday. ﻿ When asked to respond to allegations of financial mismanagement while in government, the former governor urged people in doubt to go to the state and ask questions about how resources were managed. He said he pities those who call him a thief. The former governor also described himself as a man who was blessed by God and able to meet his needs and those of his family members. Bello, who has consistently denied wrongdoing, is facing multiple cases instituted by the anti-graft agency over alleged misappropriation of public funds during his eight-year tenure as governor of the state. The EFCC Chairman, Ola Olukoyede, said in an interview with Channels Television in January 2026 that the commission had filed three cases against the former governor and fulfilled its mandate by investigating and prosecuting him. According to Olukoyede, the responsibility for determining Bello’s guilt rests with the judiciary. One of the cases involves a 16-count charge bordering on alleged criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving ₦110.4 billion. Bello, who was the governor from 2016 to 2024, is standing trial alongside two former state government officials. The Federal Government alleges that the defendants diverted state funds to acquire properties in highbrow areas of Abuja and Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Bello is also facing a separate 19-count charge involving an alleged ₦80.2 billion fraud and money laundering before the Federal High Court in Abuja. However, some prosecution witnesses have given evidence that has featured prominently in the proceedings. In February 2026, an EFCC witness, Olomotane Egoro, told the Federal High Court that Bello’s name did not appear as a beneficiary, signatory, or party to transactions involving some companies allegedly awarded local government contracts in Kogi State. Similarly, in March, another prosecution witness, Mahmoud Abdulazeez, maintained that Bello’s name was not linked to the transactions involving property documents tendered before the court. In June 2026, the 17th prosecution witness, Shehu Bala, also told the court during cross-examination that Bello was not involved in the property transactions under examination. Meanwhile, the EFCC secured a significant legal victory in August 2025 when the Court of Appeal in Lagos restored an interim forfeiture order covering 14 properties allegedly linked to the former governor. item.title: The Other Black Gold: Nigeria’s Coffee Sector Wants A Shot
item.description: Richard Ali grew up with the aroma of coffee wafting through his house in central Nigeria as his father, an accountant, worked late into the night, drinking powdered, instant stuff from Maxwell House and Nescafé. It was not until years later, travelling on the other side of the continent, that Ali had a taste of “coffee, coffee — brewed coffee”. “I have to bring this to Nigeria,” he thought, and he started looking into importing beans from Rwanda. Ali later discovered he did not have to: coffee has been growing in Nigeria for more than 100 years. A wave of entrepreneurs in Africa’s most populous country are turning towards the oil-producing nation’s other black gold — an uphill task in a place full of tea and instant coffee, and little sense of homegrown java as a daily staple or part of a wider cultural patrimony. A general view of someone handling coffee beans in a plantation in the Gorongosa mountain range in Gorongosa on May 20, 2022. (Photo by Alfredo Zuniga / AFP) But roasters say they have found a market — and sense of national pride — to tap into, even if Nigeria’s beans are not well-known. “We need to grow more coffee, whether for the domestic market, which is expanding, or the global market, which is now considering Nigerian coffee,” Ali, founder of Tigray Coffee, which launched in 2021, said over a cup of Nigerian brew, light with slightly chocolatey notes. Agricultural Investments In Ethiopia, hundreds of years of cultivation have bound coffee to local culture, while Uganda and Ivory Coast have become modern export powerhouses. Nigeria produced 1,808 tonnes of beans in 2024, according to statistics from the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organisation — a paltry sum compared to Kenya’s 49,500 tonnes that same year. The first seeds hit the ground in Nigeria in the 19th century, after coffee was introduced by British colonists. The crop is notoriously fickle and can only grow in certain parts of the country. But there has also been a dearth of investment in agriculture, critics say, as the government instead became over-reliant on the oil sector for revenues. Experts have long called for a more diversified economy. The government agrees, at least in principle: in May, agriculture minister Abubakar Kyari announced federal investments in coffee production in Ondo State, calling it “a powerful economic crop” that could create jobs and “boost rural livelihoods”. ‘Never Imported Coffee’ At the opening of a new cafe in Lagos last month, Princess Adeyinka Tekenah paired a local brew not with croissants, but puff-puff, a staple street food snack of fried dough. “I have been in the business for 12 years, and I have never imported coffee,” the founder of Happy Coffee said. While Tekenah has leaned into her local roots, the coffee industry has also been helped by a growing sense of cosmopolitanism in Nigeria’s cities, Ali said.
